STERNUM (Greek sternum= breastbone)
Has three parts:
1. Manubrium sterni (Latin manubrium = handle):
• Contains a notch superiorly; the jugular or suprasternal notch and articular surfaces on either side of
this notch for articulation with the clavicle at the sternoclavicular joints.
• Just inferior to these clavicular surfaces are facets for articulation with the 1st costal cartilage.
• Below that, at the lower end of the manubrium, laterally are demi-facets for articulation with the
upper half of the 2nd costal cartilage.
2. Body of sternum:
Articulates with the manubrium at the manubriosternal joint (fibrous joint); also known as the sternal
angle (of Louis); an important landmark in the thorax (marks the site on the anterior chest wall where
the sternum articulates with the 2nd costal cartilage and the 2nd rib; important for counting ribs
during a physical examination).
• Laterally has a demi-facet for articulation with the lower half of the 2nd costal cartilage and full
facets for articulation with costal cartilages of ribs 3 to 6.
• Has a demi-facet at its inferior end for articulation with upper half of 7th costal cartilage.
• Inferior end articulates with the xiphoid process at the xiphisternal joint.
3. Xiphoid Process (Greek xiphoid = like a sword):
• Small, pointed, inferior portion of the sternum.
• Shape and size are variable: may be pointed, curved anteriorly, bifid, perforated, etc.
• Has demi-facet on each side for articulation with lower half of 7th costal cartilage
Dr Atif and Dr Sadia

CLASSIFICATION OF RIBS
A. According to features
1. Typical ribs: 3rd-9th.
2. Atypical ribs: 1st, 2nd, 10th, 11th, and 12th.
The typical ribs have same general features, whereas the atypical ribs have special features and
therefore can be
differentiated from the remaining ribs.
B. According to relation with the sternum
1. True ribs: 1st-7th (i.e., upper 7 ribs).
2. False ribs: 8th-12th (i.e., lower 5 ribs).
True ribs articulate with the sternum anteriorly, whereas false ribs do not articulate with the
sternum anteriorly.
C. According to articulation
1. Vertebro sternal ribs: 1st-7th.
2. Vertebro chondral ribs: 8th-10th.
3. Vertebral (floating) ribs: 11th and 12th.

Typical Ribs
A typical rib consists of the following parts:
Head (posterior; articulates with demi-facets on two adjacent thoracic vertebral bodies I except ribs
1, 10, 11 and 12])
Neck (narrowed portion just distal to the head) Curved shaft (posterior, lateral, and anterior)
Tubercle (bony prominence between the neck and the shaft that articulates with the transverse
process of a thoracic vertebra)
Rounded superior margin
Sharp inferior margin (marked by costal groove on its internal surface for the intercostal
neurovascular bundle)
Angle (where the shaft bends sharply anteriorly just distal to the tubercle)
Sternal end (anterior end that articulates with the sternum through a costal cartilage

Surface features of the Atypical rib (1)
1st Rib:
• Shorter, thicker and stronger than the rest of the ribs
• Head articulates with T 1 vertebral body through a single articular facet
• Characterized by a bony protuberance, the scalene tubercle, on its superior surface for the
Ittachment of the scalenus anterior muscle
Scalene tubercle separates two smooth grooves on the superior surface of the rib: a groove
terior to it for the subclavian vein and a groove posterior to it for the subclavian artery
• Scalenus medius muscle attached to upper surface posterior to the groove for the subclavian
artery

ribs (3 through 10)
• Anterior ends are pointed
• Have no anterior attachments; end in
anterolateral abdominal wall muscles

Typical Thoracic Vertebra
Inferior
articular process
Consists of the following parts:
• Heart-shaped vertebral body anteriorly; has demi-facets for articulation with heads of ribs (except TI,
TIO, TI 1 and TI 2, which have full facets).
• Circular vertebral foramen (houses spinal cord and its coverings, roots of thoracic spinal nerves, epidural
fat and internal vertebral venous plexus).
• Long spinous process posteriorly angled inferiorly.
• Transverse processes laterally that are angled posteriorly (have articular facets for articulation with
tubercles of ribs) (except TI 1 and TI2).
• Broad, flat, overlapping laminae (overlap with lamina of vertebra below) connecting the transverse processes
with the spinous process (Latin lamina = plate or wall)
• Short, thick pedicles Connecting the vertebral body with the transverse
processes.
• Superior articular process: projects superiorly with articular facet oriented almost vertically and
facing posteriorly.
• Inferior articular process: projects inferiorly with articular facet facing anteriorly; the superior
articular process of one vertebra articulates with the inferior articular process of the vertebra above through
their articular facets at the zygapophyseal or facet joints.
The facet joints are synovial joints with a synovial joint cavity and fibrous joint capsule reinforced with
ligaments.
